data.title: Wall Street stocks in relief rally after heavy AI-related selloff
data.description:
Key points:
  • Benchmark S&P 500 and Nasdaq rise; Dow edges lower
  • Japan, Korea, Taiwan plunged in Asia, European stocks fall
  • Bonds take breather as US payrolls top forecasts
  • Oil set for biggest weekly drop since COVID plunge

By Chibuike Oguh and Marc Jones

Wall Street equities mostly rallied on Friday, reversing course after trillions of dollars of world stock market value was wiped out over fears that Democratic election victories this week would bring tighter US regulations for the AI industry.

Benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were trading higher with technology, communication services and consumer discretionary stocks driving gains. The Dow edged lower on the day. All three indexes were on track for weekly losses following a brutal selloff in the prior session.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.08%, the S&P 500 CBOE:SPX rose 0.71%, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.4%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was up 4.2% after slumping in its biggest one-day drop since April 2025. Nvidia rose 3%, after suffering its worst day since January 2025, when the emergence of low-cost Chinese AI model DeepSeek hammered markets.

Other heavyweight chipmakers, including AMD , Intel , and Micron Technology , were up between 5.5% and 10%, while Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were also up 2% and 8% respectively after losses earlier this week.

"Most of the disruption of the AI buildout will not probably occur but it's just the uncertainty of the change in government from Republican-led to Democratic-led, not only at the federal level but the state, local levels," said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at Sparrow Capital Management.

"That's causing some disruption in the expectations of investors... The volatility around elections or any political event, whether it be war or terrorist attack, is always going to disrupt the market."

Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said on Thursday that the state — which already has a large share of US data centres — will introduce new laws to protect local communities from their further mass buildup.

The jitters are hitting an AI trade already under pressure from fears that the massive cost of the data centres and other infrastructure will limit future returns, spurring margin calls and spooking retail investors and hedge funds alike.

RIPPLE EFFECT

The bounces were in stark contrast with market action in the rest of the world. Europe's STOXX 600 lost 1%. In Asia, Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's KOSPI both slumped about 6%. For the Nikkei — just like Wall Street the previous day — it was the biggest one-day drop since US President Donald Trump's "Liberation Day" trade tariff panic of April 2025.

The MSCI All-World index EURONEXT:IACWI fell 0.52% while MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) lost 3%.

PAYROLLS BEAT FORECASTS

US nonfarm payrolls, usually one of the most-focused on pieces of data, but largely overshadowed by the tech drama, showed a stronger-than-expected 165,000 pickup in jobs.

An anticipated slowdown in annual wage growth to below 3% for the first time in nearly 5-1/2 years did not materialise either as it came in at 3.1%.

The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note ticked up to 4.85%, having dropped to its lowest level since September 9 overnight.

In currencies, the dollar rose against major currencies including the euro, yen and Swiss franc. It was up 0.52% against the yen and rose 0.47% against the Swiss franc . The euro was down 0.68% against the dollar at $1.1142.

Brent crude prices tiptoed back up towards $100 a barrel, but are still set for their biggest weekly drop since 2020 on hopes the midterms' results might prompt Trump to de-escalate the Iran war.

Spot gold fell 0.48% to $4,067.75.

data.title: CBOT corn creeps higher before USDA crop data next week
data.description:
Chicago Board of Trade corn futures finished slightly higher on short covering and technical buying on Friday in a rebound from four-month lows reached this week, analysts said.

  • Traders were waiting for the US Department of Agriculture to update crop estimates in a monthly report due on Tuesday.

  • The USDA will use an artificial intelligence tool to check next week's crop production report after errors in corn data from September, agency officials said.

  • The USDA is expected to peg the nation's corn harvest at 15.962 billion bushels, down from its October estimate of 16.034 billion, according to a Reuters poll of analysts.

  • The harvest would be the second largest in history, after last year's record crop.

  • Drier weather will be favorable for farmers' remaining corn and soybean harvests next week, after rains delayed harvesting in some areas this week, forecasters said.

  • CBOT December corn (CZ26) ended up 1-1/2 cents at $4.41-1/2 per bushel after falling earlier to $4.38-1/2, which matched a four-month low set on Wednesday.

  • For the week, the contract dropped about 1.4%.

data.title: Alphabet's Drone Unit to Invest Up to $125M in New Texas Manufacturing Facility
data.description:
(19:45 GMT) *Alphabet's Wing to Invest Up to $125M in Direct Manufacturing Over Next Two Years
(19:45 GMT) *Wing's Manufacturing Investment Anchored by New Facility in Fort Worth, Texas
(19:45 GMT) *Wing to Invest in R&D, Engineering Capabilities in California
(19:45 GMT) Alphabet's Drone Unit to Invest Up to $125M in New Texas Manufacturing Facility

By Kelly Cloonan

Wing, the drone division of Alphabet Inc., is investing up to $125 million over the next two years in a new manufacturing facility as it looks to meet growing demand for quicker delivery.

The plant, to be located in Fort Worth, Texas, would have the capacity to build tens of thousands of aircraft each year, Wing said Friday.

The facility aims to support Wing's efforts to expand its delivery services across the U.S. The company is aiming to scale to nearly 20 U.S. markets by 2027 through its partnership with Walmart, up from a current footprint of five major metropolitan areas, including the Dallas-Fort Worth, Atlanta and Houston.

The move comes as drones gain momentum in the U.S. as the technology advances, and as retailers look for faster ways to make deliveries.

"Drone delivery has become a global reality, driven by clear demand from our partners and their customers," Wing Chief Executive Adam Woodworth said.

Wing said the new, 15,000-square-foot Texas facility would create up to 100 manufacturing jobs.

Like Wing, startup Zipline has similarly signed a series of deals with commercial partners such as Walmart and Uber Technologies' Uber Eats, and on Thursday announced new funding that more than doubles its valuation from earlier this year, to $21.5 billion. Amazon.com and delivery company DoorDash also have their own in-house drone divisions.

Write to Kelly Cloonan at kelly.cloonan@wsj.com
